title: Logic Gates: AND, OR, XOR & Friends
oneLiner: Every computation a CPU does eventually reduces to these tiny truth-table circuits, wired together by the billions.
keyTakeaway: A transistor is just an electronic switch; wire a handful of them together in a specific pattern and you get a logic gate that implements one rule of Boolean logic (true/false logic, named after the mathematician George Boole) (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, ...). Wire enough gates together and you get an adder, then an ALU (the arithmetic logic unit, the part of the CPU that does the math), then a CPU -- there's no magic step in between arithmetic and "a bunch of switches," just more of the same pattern.
explanation: Zoom all the way into a CPU and every wire is either high voltage or low voltage -- true or false, 1 or 0. A logic gate is a tiny circuit (built from a handful of transistors) that takes one or two of those true/false inputs and produces a true/false output according to a fixed rule: AND is true only if both inputs are true; OR is true if either is; NOT flips a single input; XOR ("exclusive or") is true only if the inputs DISAGREE, which makes it the gate behind binary addition (adding two bits without a carry is exactly XOR) and behind detecting "did this bit flip" in error-checking and cryptography. NAND and NOR are AND/OR with the output flipped -- and NAND in particular is special: every other gate (including AND, OR, and NOT) can be built out of nothing but NAND gates, so in principle a whole chip could be built from NAND alone, and NAND is one of the cheapest, most common cells in CMOS logic. Chain gates together and you get bigger behavior for free: a "half adder" (add two bits, produce a sum bit and a carry bit) is just one XOR gate and one AND gate; combine two half adders (plus an OR gate) into a "full adder" that also accepts a carry-in, and chain eight full adders to add two whole bytes. This is the actual bridge between "physics" and "software": there is no separate layer where numbers or logic get invented -- it's gates, all the way up.
